topics.title: Sources of Law, Intentional Torts & Privacy
topics.summary: Nursing practice is shaped by constitutional, statutory, administrative, and common law; criminal law protects society, while civil law (including torts) lets an injured individual sue. Intentional torts — assault, battery, false imprisonment, defamation, and invasion of privacy — are willful acts the nurse can prevent by obtaining consent, using the least restrictive approach, and protecting health information.
objectives: Distinguish constitutional, statutory, administrative, and common law and give a nursing example of each.
Explain how the Nurse Practice Act (statute) and the Board of Nursing (administrative agency) work together to regulate licensure and scope.
Differentiate criminal law from civil law, and felonies from misdemeanors, and recognize that one act can trigger criminal, civil, and licensure consequences at the same time.
Classify a bedside scenario as assault, battery, false imprisonment, defamation, or invasion of privacy, and choose the action that prevents it.
Apply HIPAA and confidentiality rules to phone calls, visitors, electronic records, and social media.
Select the legally and ethically correct nursing response when a competent client refuses care or wants to leave against medical advice.
topics.bigPicture:
Law can feel far away from the bedside, but almost every nursing action has a legal frame. The license you earn is granted by a state statute (the Nurse Practice Act). The rules that tell you what an RN may and may not do are written by an administrative agency (the Board of Nursing). And every time you touch a client, close a door, apply a restraint, chart a note, or answer a phone call about a client, you are acting inside tort and privacy law. Knowing the categories is not about becoming a lawyer — it is about recognizing when an ordinary-looking action crosses a line.

The NCLEX rarely asks “Which branch of government makes statutes?” Instead, it describes a nurse who says “If you don’t take this pill, I’ll have to give you a shot,” a confused client tied to a chair without an order, a nurse reading her neighbor’s chart, or a client walking toward the exit against medical advice — and asks you to name the problem or choose the safe, legal response. The winning pattern is almost always the same: respect the competent client’s right to decide, get consent before touching, use the least restrictive measure, share only the minimum necessary information with people who need it, and escalate through the chain of command.

This topic gives you the vocabulary (law, statutes, administrative law, crime, civil law, tort) and then the intentional torts in detail. The companion topics cover the unintentional tort of negligence/malpractice and the specific laws on consent, minors, controlled substances, Good Samaritan care, whistleblowing, and abuse reporting.

keyTerms.def: The sum total of the rules and regulations by which a society is governed (Guido, 2020). Laws are made at federal, state, and local levels and change as societal needs change.

The U.S. Constitution grants the federal government power to make laws; states keep inherent power to protect health, safety, public order, and welfare. Examples affecting nurses: due process and equal protection.

Laws enacted by legislative bodies (Congress, state legislatures, city/county governments). The Nurse Practice Act is a state statutory law; others include statutes of limitation, protection/reporting laws, natural death acts, informed consent laws, Good Samaritan acts, advance directive laws, and the ADA.

Rules and regulations made by administrative agencies that a legislature has authorized to interpret and enforce a statute. The state Board of Nursing is an administrative agency that interprets and enforces the Nurse Practice Act.
Law derived from judicial decisions and court rulings (precedent) rather than from written statutes.
The state statute that defines nursing, sets licensure requirements and scope of practice for each level of nurse, and establishes grounds for discipline.
Public law that defines conduct harmful to another person or to society as a whole, punishable by fines or imprisonment, and enforced by law enforcement and government prosecutors.

An act prohibited by statute or common-law principles that is considered an offense against the state rather than only the individual. Classified as felonies (more serious, e.g., homicide, manslaughter, major theft) or misdemeanors (lesser offenses).
Private law dealing with the rights and duties of private individuals; most often enforced through lawsuits seeking compensation (contracts and torts).

A civil wrong committed against an individual or an individual’s property, for which the injured person may sue and be awarded compensation. Torts are unintentional (negligence/malpractice) or intentional.

A willful act — the person intended to perform the action — that violates another’s rights (assault, battery, false imprisonment, defamation, invasion of privacy). Intent to act, not intent to harm, is what matters.
Creating an apprehension (reasonable fear) of offensive, insulting, or physically injurious touching. No actual touching is required (e.g., threatening a client who refuses an IV).

Willful touching of another person (or their clothing or something they are carrying) that is unwanted, embarrassing, or unwarranted — e.g., an injection without consent or forcing a client to ambulate against their will.

The unjustifiable detention of a person without legal warrant to confine the person — e.g., confining a client to a room, restraining without an order/justification, or blocking a competent client from leaving AMA.
A false statement communicated to a third party that damages a person’s reputation. Libel is written (including charting, email, social media); slander is spoken.
Unauthorized intrusion into a person’s private affairs or disclosure of private information — including name, photos, video, personal belongings, personal space, and immediate territory.

Federal rule that sets minimum standards for protecting Protected Health Information (PHI): physical/mental conditions, services provided, payment, name, address, birth date, Social Security number, and other identifiers. A stricter (more protective) state law or facility policy is followed when it exists.
Civil law governing agreements, such as nurse–employer, nurse–client, nurse–insurer, and client–agency relationships.

sections.heading: Where nursing law comes from: four sources
sections.body:
Think of the legal system as layers. At the top is the Constitution, which sets the ground rules for government and protects rights such as due process and equal protection. The Constitution lets states act to protect the health, safety, and welfare of their residents — and licensing nurses is one way states do that.

Next come statutory laws, written by elected legislatures. Every state has a Nurse Practice Act (NPA), which is a statute. Legislatures also pass statutes of limitation, child and adult abuse reporting laws, Good Samaritan acts, natural death and advance directive acts, informed consent laws, sexual harassment laws, and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Legislatures cannot write every detail, so they delegate authority to agencies. Those agencies write administrative laws (rules and regulations) that have the force of law. The Board of Nursing is the administrative agency that interprets and enforces the NPA: it licenses nurses, writes scope-of-practice rules, approves nursing programs, investigates complaints, and disciplines licenses.

Finally, common law comes from judges. When a court decides a case, its reasoning becomes precedent that later courts follow. Much of tort law — what counts as negligence or battery, and what a “reasonable” nurse would do — grew from court decisions rather than statutes.

sections.analogy: Think of a board game. The Constitution is the box that says what game you are playing and who may play. The statute (NPA) is the official rulebook printed by the game company. The administrative rules are the detailed FAQ the referee (the Board) publishes to explain how the rulebook applies. Common law is the list of past referee calls that everyone now follows when the same situation comes up again.

sections.heading: The Nurse Practice Act and the Board of Nursing: statute vs. agency
sections.body:
Students often blur these two. The NPA is the law itself, passed by the legislature; it defines nursing, creates the Board, sets education and licensure requirements, and lists grounds for discipline. The Board of Nursing is the agency the NPA creates. Its rules (administrative law) fill in the details — for example, exactly what an RN versus an LPN may do, how delegation must occur, and how complaints are evaluated.

Why does this matter at the bedside? Because the NPA and Board rules are the primary legal basis of your standard of care and scope of practice. An employer’s job description and policies can limit what you do, but they can never expand your scope beyond what the NPA allows. If a manager asks an LPN to perform an initial admission assessment that the state reserves for RNs, the policy does not protect the LPN — the NPA controls. Nurses must also keep current, because NPAs and rules change.

Healthcare policies sit below laws. Agency policies exist to (1) promote client safety and reduce errors that cause adverse events and (2) protect staff and the agency as a whole — for instance, a policy on inventorying client valuables prevents theft or accidental loss and protects the nurse from accusations. Clients, in turn, have rights: a privilege, demand, or claim by virtue of law to expect competent nursing services.
sections.example: A new graduate is told by a charge nurse, “Our unit policy lets the nurse aides adjust IV pump rates when they’re busy.” The nurse recognizes that policy cannot authorize something outside the aide’s legal scope or the Board’s delegation rules. She does not delegate the task, follows the chain of command to clarify the policy, and uses the agency’s quality-improvement process to flag the conflict.

check.q: A hospital job description lists a task that the state’s Board of Nursing rules do not allow an LPN to perform. Which rule controls the LPN’s practice?
check.a: The Nurse Practice Act and Board rules. An employer may restrict scope but cannot expand it beyond the NPA, so the LPN should decline the task and notify the supervisor.

sections.heading: Public vs. private law: criminal, civil, contracts, and torts
sections.body:
Criminal law is public law. The wrong is treated as an offense against the state or society, and the government (a prosecutor) brings the case. Punishment is a fine or imprisonment. Crimes are felonies (more serious: homicide, manslaughter, major theft, arson, sexual assault) or misdemeanors (lesser offenses). Crimes that directly involve nurses include diverting or illegally possessing controlled substances, active euthanasia, sexual assault of a client, and theft of client property.

Civil law is private law between individuals. The injured person (plaintiff) sues the person they believe caused the harm (defendant), usually for money (damages). Civil law includes contracts (nurse–employer, nurse–client, nurse–insurer, client–agency) and torts. A tort is a civil wrong against a person or their property: negligence/malpractice, libel and slander, invasion of privacy, assault and battery, false imprisonment, and abandonment.

One action can trigger three separate systems at once. A nurse who steals a client’s oxycodone and replaces it with saline may face (1) criminal prosecution for drug diversion, (2) a civil lawsuit from the client who suffered uncontrolled pain, and (3) administrative action by the Board of Nursing against the license. Being found “not guilty” in criminal court does not automatically protect the license, because each system uses its own standards.

check.q: A client sues a nurse for posting a photo of the client’s wound on social media. Is this criminal or civil, and which category?
check.a: Civil — it is a tort (invasion of privacy) brought by the individual. It may also be a HIPAA violation and grounds for Board discipline, which are separate consequences.

sections.heading: Intentional torts: the key is intent to act, not intent to harm
sections.body:
Unintentional torts (negligence and malpractice) happen when a nurse falls below the standard of care without meaning to — forgetting to raise side rails, giving the wrong dose. Intentional torts are different: the nurse meant to perform the action. The nurse may have had good motives (“I gave the shot because he really needed it”), but a good motive does not erase the tort. That willful nature is what separates intentional torts from negligence, and it is why intentional torts can lead to both civil suits and, in some cases, criminal charges.

Assault is creating apprehension of harmful or offensive touching. The client must reasonably fear being touched; actual contact is not needed. Saying “If you don’t hold still, I’ll strap you down,” or approaching with a syringe after the client says no, can be assault. Battery is the unwanted, unwarranted, or embarrassing touching itself — including touching the client’s clothing or something they are holding. Giving an injection without consent, inserting a catheter after the client refused, forcing a client to walk against their will, or continuing a procedure after consent is withdrawn are all battery — even if the treatment was medically beneficial and caused no harm.

How do nurses avoid these torts? Explain what you are about to do and obtain consent (a nod or holding out an arm can be implied consent for routine care; procedures need informed consent). If a client refuses, stop, explore the reason, provide information, and notify the provider. Document the refusal and the teaching. Never threaten or coerce.
sections.example: A client refuses his 0900 enoxaparin injection, saying the bruises hurt. The nurse says, “That’s fine — but I’ll have to tell your doctor you’re being difficult, and you might need a shot in the stomach every hour then.” This is coercive and could be assault. The correct response: acknowledge the concern, explain the purpose (preventing clots), offer measures such as rotating sites, respect the refusal if he still declines, notify the provider, and document.

check.q: A nurse holds the arm of a competent client who is pulling away and administers an IM antiemetic “to help her.” Which tort, and why doesn’t the good intention matter?
check.a: Battery. The nurse intended the touch, and the client did not consent. Intent to act — not intent to harm — defines an intentional tort.

sections.heading: False imprisonment: restraints, seclusion, and the client who wants to leave
sections.body:
False imprisonment is the unjustified detention of a person without legal authority. It includes confining a client to a room, restraining a client to a bed or chair to restrict freedom without an order or clinical justification, and detaining a competent client who wishes to leave against medical advice (AMA). Physically blocking the door, hiding a client’s clothes or keys, or threatening to call security to keep a competent client from leaving all fit.

Restraints are legal when they are justified and ordered: a provider order (or emergency application per policy with a prompt order), used only when less restrictive measures have failed and the client is at imminent risk of harming self or others, time-limited, with ongoing monitoring and documentation. Using restraints for staff convenience or as punishment is never justified. Legal holds also exist — for example, an involuntary psychiatric commitment ordered under state law, or a court order — and detention under a valid hold is not false imprisonment.

When a competent adult wants to leave AMA, the right to refuse treatment includes the right to leave. The nurse cannot physically stop them. The nurse can, and should, try to understand why, help resolve the concern if possible, make sure the client understands the risks, and involve the provider.
steps: Ensure immediate safety and ask, calmly and privately, why the client wants to leave — often the reason (pain, a sick pet, a billing fear, waiting time) can be solved.
Assess decision-making capacity: is the client alert, oriented, and able to understand the risks? Confusion, intoxication, or acute psychosis changes the situation — follow policy and get help.
Notify the provider promptly so the risks can be explained and alternatives offered.
Explain the risks of leaving in plain language; offer the AMA form. The client may refuse to sign — that is also their right.
Do not block exits, take belongings, or threaten; never restrain a competent adult to keep them.
Remove IV access and devices safely if the client is leaving; provide discharge information and instructions to return.
Document the conversation, capacity findings, provider notification, risks explained, the client’s words, and the time of departure.

check.q: A confused older adult keeps trying to climb out of bed. The nurse asks a coworker for a vest restraint “just until shift change.” What is the legal problem, and what should happen instead?
check.a: Restraining without an order or attempted less-restrictive alternatives risks false imprisonment (and harm). Assess the cause of the behavior, try alternatives (toileting, bed alarm, low bed, frequent rounding, a sitter, reorientation), and contact the provider if restraint seems necessary.

sections.heading: Defamation and invasion of privacy
sections.body:
Defamation is communicating a false statement to a third party that harms someone’s reputation. Libel is written — including chart notes, emails, incident reports, texts, and social media. Slander is spoken. Charting “Client is a drug seeker and a liar” is subjective, unprofessional, and potentially libelous; charting the objective facts (“Client requested hydromorphone at 1300 and 1400; states pain 8/10; grimacing; provider notified”) is defensible. Gossiping at the nurses’ station that a coworker “comes to work drunk” without facts is potential slander — concerns about impairment must go through proper reporting channels, not the hallway.

Invasion of privacy covers both information and territory. Confidential client information may not be disclosed without authorization, and that includes the client’s name, photographs, and video recordings. Privacy also includes control of personal belongings, personal space, and immediate territory. Searching a client’s room or belongings, touching personal items without permission, or entering a room without knocking can violate that trust. (The course notes that the Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches; in healthcare, privacy rights are also protected by HIPAA, state law, and tort law.)

When a room search is genuinely needed for safety (for example, suspected weapons on a behavioral health unit), follow agency policy exactly: a clear safety reason, proper authorization, the client present when possible, a witness, and documentation.
sections.example: A nursing student photographs a client’s unusual tattoo “for a care-plan presentation,” cropping out the face. Even without the face, a distinctive tattoo can identify the client, and no authorization was obtained. The student should delete the photo, notify the instructor, and follow the agency’s reporting process.

sections.heading: HIPAA in daily practice: who may know what
sections.body:
HIPAA’s Privacy Rule protects PHI: physical and mental conditions, services provided, payment information, and identifiers such as name, address, birth date, and Social Security number. It sets the minimum federal standard; when a state law or facility policy is more protective, the stricter rule is followed.

Three ideas solve most NCLEX privacy items. First, need to know: only members of the care team who need the information for treatment, payment, or operations access it, and they access only the minimum necessary. Looking up a celebrity, coworker, family member, or neighbor you are not caring for is a violation — even if you never tell anyone. Second, the client controls disclosure to family and friends: ask the client who may receive information; use agency passcodes or identity checks for phone calls; if the client says not to share, don’t. Third, some disclosures are required by law without authorization — suspected child or vulnerable-adult abuse, certain communicable diseases, and other mandatory reports — and these are exceptions to confidentiality.

Why this matters to you personally: a single unauthorized disclosure can trigger three separate consequences at once — a civil lawsuit by the client for invasion of privacy, federal HIPAA penalties (civil fines, and criminal penalties for knowingly obtaining or disclosing PHI), and Board of Nursing discipline for unprofessional conduct. An employer’s curiosity or “safety concern” does not authorize disclosure of an employee’s diagnosis, and Good Samaritan laws have nothing to do with privacy. When a coworker breaches privacy (for example, a social media post), report it through the chain of command and agency policy rather than replying publicly or ignoring it.

Protect electronic records: log off or lock screens, never share passwords, position screens away from visitors, and do not discuss clients in elevators, cafeterias, or on social media (even without names). Teach clients how privacy is protected and discuss care only with appropriate people.

check.q: A nurse sees her neighbor’s name on the unit census, opens his chart briefly “to make sure he’s okay,” and tells no one. Has she violated privacy law?
check.a: Yes. Accessing PHI without a work-related need is a breach, even if nothing is disclosed. Access logs show who opened the record.

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: These pairs are where students lose points. Find the one clue that separates them.

rows: Assault vs. battery
Assault = threat that creates fear of touch; battery = the actual unwanted touch
“Threatens,” “if you don’t…” → assault; “administers,” “holds down,” “forces” → battery
Battery vs. negligence
Battery is an intended touch without consent; negligence is an unintended failure to meet the standard
Did the nurse mean to do the act? Yes → intentional tort
False imprisonment vs. appropriate restraint
Restraint with an order, justification, least-restrictive trial, and monitoring is lawful
“No order,” “for convenience,” “competent client wants to leave” → false imprisonment
Libel vs. slander
Libel is written (charting, posts); slander is spoken
Look for “documents,” “posts,” “emails” vs. “tells,” “says”

Reporting suspected abuse or reportable disease is required, not a breach
“Suspects abuse,” “reportable disease” → report

Legislature writes statutes (NPA); agency (BON) writes rules to implement them
“Act” vs. “Board rule/regulation”
