sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: intentional torts and privacy
sections.body:
Expect three patterns. (1) Name the tort: a short scenario and four labels (assault, battery, false imprisonment, invasion of privacy). Ask yourself: Was there a threat only, an actual touch, a restriction of movement, or information/territory exposed? (2) Best response or action: a client refuses care or wants to leave AMA, or a family member asks for information. The correct answer respects the competent client’s autonomy, explores the reason, notifies the provider, and documents — it never threatens, restrains, or discloses. (3) Needs further teaching: a new nurse lists privacy practices; one statement (e.g., “I can look up my patient’s family member if they ask me to”) is wrong.

Sample item (original): A client who is alert and oriented tells the nurse, “I’m done. I’m going home right now,” and begins to dress. The client has a heparin infusion running for a pulmonary embolism. Which action should the nurse take first? A. Tell the client security will be called if they try to leave. B. Ask the client what is prompting the decision to leave now. C. Clamp the IV and remove the catheter so the client can leave safely. D. Have the client sign the against-medical-advice form.
steps: Read the stem: competent (alert, oriented) adult; wants to leave; serious condition; the word “first.”
Identify what is being asked: the first action when a competent client wants to leave AMA — a communication/assessment step comes before procedures or paperwork.
Spot cues: “alert and oriented” means the client has the right to leave; the heparin drip means leaving is dangerous, so the nurse wants to understand and possibly resolve the concern.
Eliminate A: threatening security to keep a competent client is coercion that can constitute assault and false imprisonment.
Eliminate C: removing the IV is a later step once the client has truly decided to leave and the provider is notified; doing it first skips exploring the reason.
Eliminate D: the AMA form comes after the risks are explained and the provider is involved; it is not the first action and the client may decline to sign.
Choose B: exploring the reason is assessment, may resolve the problem, and respects autonomy. Next steps: notify the provider, explain risks, document.
bullets: Reusable strategy: when a competent client refuses or wants to leave, the first answer is usually “explore/assess the reason,” then “notify the provider,” then “explain risks/document.” Any option that threatens, restrains, or forces is wrong.

sections.heading: Worked case: the refused catheter and the curious visitor
sections.body: Mrs. Alvarez, 72, is admitted with urinary retention after surgery. She is alert and oriented. The provider orders a straight catheterization. When the nurse enters with the kit, Mrs. Alvarez says, “No — I don’t want that tube. Let me try again on my own.” A nursing assistant says, “She’ll thank us later. I’ll hold her legs and you just do it.” Twenty minutes later, a man at the desk says he is her son and asks what surgery she had and “whether it was cancer.”
steps: Recognize cues: competent client, explicit refusal; coworker proposing to hold her; an unverified caller asking for diagnosis details.

Analyze: proceeding would be battery (unwanted touch), and holding her down adds a restraint without justification. Telling the coworker “Let’s just do it” would also make the nurse responsible for the assistant’s action.

Act on the refusal: stop, thank her for telling you, explore the reason (embarrassment? pain? fear?), and offer alternatives she can try — privacy, running water, positioning, a bladder scan to measure volume.
Communicate: notify the provider of the refusal and the bladder scan results; the provider may discuss risks and options with her.
Educate the assistant privately that consent can be refused or withdrawn at any time and that forcing care is battery.

Handle the visitor: do not confirm details. Check whether Mrs. Alvarez has listed him as someone who may receive information, or ask her directly whether she wants information shared. If she agrees, share within her wishes; if not, tell the visitor kindly that you cannot share and suggest he speak with her.
Document objectively: the refusal in her words, teaching, alternatives tried, bladder scan result, provider notification, and her response.

check.q: Mrs. Alvarez later agrees to the catheterization, then halfway through says, “Stop, it hurts too much.” What should the nurse do?
check.a: Stop the procedure. Consent can be withdrawn at any time; continuing would be battery. Assess her pain, reassure her, and notify the provider about the incomplete procedure.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
In North Carolina, nursing is regulated by the North Carolina Board of Nursing (NCBON) under the NC Nursing Practice Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 90, Article 9A, G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) — that is the statute. The NCBON’s rules in the North Carolina Administrative Code are the administrative law layer; RN components of practice are in 21 NCAC 36 .0224 and LPN components in 21 NCAC 36 .0225. The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment; the LPN participates under RN or provider supervision. The NCBON publishes scope-of-practice and delegation decision trees to help nurses decide whether an activity is within scope.

North Carolina is a Nurse Licensure Compact state, so an NC multistate license allows practice in other compact states — but the nurse must follow the practice laws of the state where the client is located.

Conduct issues such as drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, and confidentiality breaches are reported to the NCBON rather than handled only by the employer. Child maltreatment reports go to the county department of social services (DSS) director under G.S. 7B-301. NC is a universal reporting state: any person or institution with cause to suspect abuse, neglect, or dependency of a juvenile must report — not only nurses — and knowingly failing to report is a crime. Reports of a disabled adult in need of protective services also go to the county DSS director (G.S. 108A-102). These mandatory reports are legal exceptions to confidentiality, so making them is never a privacy violation. The NCLEX itself is national and will not ask statute numbers — know them for your practice, and answer NCLEX items with national principles.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 49 study guide, pp. 2825–2827 (foundational overview, sources of law, Figure 49.1, public vs. private law, Table 49.1) and pp. 2828–2829 (intentional torts, defamation, invasion of privacy, HIPAA Privacy Rule).

Clarifications: (1) The course states that invasion of privacy is protected under the Fourth Amendment. The Fourth Amendment specifically limits unreasonable government searches and seizures; in healthcare, a client’s privacy is protected mainly by HIPAA, state confidentiality laws, and the civil tort of invasion of privacy. The nursing behaviors taught here are unchanged. (2) Common law is added to the list of sources because it underlies much of tort law. (3) Restraint requirements (order, least-restrictive alternatives, monitoring) and the AMA process are standard national practice added to apply the false-imprisonment content. (4) HIPAA’s “minimum necessary” and treatment/payment/operations concepts were added as standard federal rules.

mnemonics.name: “Threat vs. Touch”
mnemonics.text: Assault = Apprehension (threat, no touch needed). Battery = Body contact without consent. If the nurse only said it, think assault; if the nurse did it, think battery.

mnemonics.name: Libel = Lasting, Slander = Spoken
mnemonics.text: Libel leaves a lasting written record (chart, email, post). Slander is spoken and disappears into the air.

pearls: A good motive never cures battery: beneficial treatment given over a competent client’s refusal is still battery.
A competent adult may leave AMA; the nurse explores the reason, notifies the provider, explains risks, and documents — never blocks the door.
The client may refuse to sign the AMA form; document that refusal too.
Employers can narrow but never widen the scope of practice the Nurse Practice Act allows.
Opening a chart you have no work reason to open is a privacy breach even if you tell no one.
Chart objective facts, not labels — subjective judgments about character can be libelous.
Mandatory reports (abuse, reportable diseases) are exceptions to confidentiality; making them is not a HIPAA violation.
One act can bring criminal charges, a civil suit, and Board discipline — three separate systems.
redFlags: Any plan to hold, tie, or sedate a competent client so care can be done “for their own good.”
A coworker suggesting restraints for convenience or without an order.
Requests for client information by phone or from visitors whose identity and authorization are not verified.
Photos, videos, or social media posts involving clients, even with faces hidden.
Threatening language (“If you don’t…, I’ll…”) used to gain cooperation.
recap: Law comes from the Constitution, statutes (NPA), administrative rules (Board of Nursing), and common law (court decisions).
The NPA is a statute; the Board of Nursing is the administrative agency that interprets and enforces it.
Criminal law protects society and is prosecuted by the state; civil law resolves private disputes through lawsuits.
Torts are civil wrongs; intentional torts are willful acts — assault, battery, false imprisonment, defamation, invasion of privacy.
Assault is the threat; battery is the unwanted touch; false imprisonment is unjustified restraint or detention.
Privacy includes information, images, belongings, and personal space; HIPAA sets the federal minimum, and stricter state law or policy wins.
Access and share PHI only on a need-to-know, minimum-necessary basis; mandatory reports are lawful exceptions.

checks.q: A nurse tells a client who refuses to take an oral antipsychotic, “If you won’t swallow it, I’ll get help and give it as a shot.” The client then swallows the pill. Has a tort occurred?
checks.a: Possibly assault — the statement created apprehension of an unwanted touch, even though no touch happened. The nurse should instead explore the refusal, educate, and notify the provider.

checks.q: An alert client with chest pain says he is leaving to pick up his child from school. List the nurse’s actions in order.
checks.a: Explore the reason and look for solutions (e.g., can someone else pick up the child?); assess capacity; notify the provider; explain risks; offer the AMA form; remove devices safely if he leaves; document.

checks.q: A Board of Nursing revokes a nurse’s license after the nurse is acquitted in a criminal diversion trial. How is this possible?
checks.a: Licensure action is administrative law, separate from criminal law, and uses its own evidence standards and grounds for discipline under the NPA.

checks.q: A client asks the nurse not to tell her husband about her pregnancy test result. The husband asks the nurse directly. What should the nurse say?
checks.a: The nurse should not disclose the result. A suitable response is that the nurse cannot share health information without the client’s permission and that he can speak with his wife.

checks.q: A nurse documents, “Daughter is obviously stealing the client’s pain pills.” What is the legal risk and the better entry?
checks.a: Possible libel (an unproven written accusation). Better: objective facts — pill count discrepancy, times, who was present, client statements — and report the concern through the proper channel.

checks.q: Which source of law is a Board of Nursing rule that defines what tasks may be delegated to assistive personnel?
checks.a: Administrative law — an agency rule implementing the statute (the Nurse Practice Act).

topics.title: Negligence, Malpractice & the Standard of Care
topics.summary: Malpractice is professional negligence: a nurse with a duty breaches the standard of care, the harm was foreseeable, the breach caused a real injury, and damages follow. Nurses prevent it by following standards, communicating and documenting defensively, advocating, supervising delegated work, reporting errors, and carrying liability insurance.
objectives: Differentiate negligence from malpractice and explain why nursing students are held to the licensed-RN standard.
Apply the six elements of malpractice (duty, breach, foreseeability, causation, injury/harm, damages) to decide whether a claim could succeed.
Classify negligent acts into the four Box 49.1 categories and identify the preventive nursing action for each.
Explain respondeat superior, res ipsa loquitur, and the statute of limitations with bedside examples.
Identify the sources that define the standard of care and resolve conflicts between policy and current practice.
Choose prevention strategies: medication safety, fall prevention, error reporting, effective communication, and defensive documentation.
Compare occurrence-based with claims-made and individual with employer-sponsored liability insurance.
topics.bigPicture:
Most lawsuits against nurses are not about dramatic intentional acts — they are about ordinary moments where something was missed: a fall-risk client left with the bed high, a rising potassium that was never called, a dose given without checking why the client was on it, a change in condition charted but not communicated. Professional nurses were responsible for 795 of 11,810 malpractice payments in the National Practitioner Data Bank in 2018, just under 7%. Behind each one is a story that usually began with a gap in assessment, communication, advocacy, or supervision.

The legal test for malpractice gives you a powerful bedside checklist. Did I have a duty to this client? Did I meet the standard a reasonably prudent nurse would meet? Could I foresee harm if I didn’t act? If harm happened, did my act or omission cause it? Thinking this way turns legal content into safe practice: you assess, you act within the standard, you escalate concerns, and you document the timeline so the record shows what you did.

On the NCLEX, this content shows up as “Which action best protects the nurse and client?”, “Which element is missing?”, “Which documentation entry is best?”, and “What should the nurse do after a medication error?” The safest answer is nearly always the one that puts client safety first, follows the standard of care, communicates clearly with the provider, and reports honestly.

keyTerms.def: Conduct that deviates from what a reasonable person (exercising average care, skill, and judgment) would do in a particular circumstance, resulting in unintended injury or property damage.

Professional negligence: conduct by a professional performing professional duties that deviates from the standard of practice dictated by the profession, measured against a reasonably skilled, competent, and experienced member of that specialty.
The state of being legally obligated and responsible. To establish malpractice liability, the plaintiff must prove all required elements.
A legally enforceable obligation to adhere to a particular standard of care; begins when the nurse accepts responsibility for providing care to a client (e.g., accepting an assignment).
A deviation from the standard of care owed to the client, by commission (doing something wrong, e.g., wrong drug) or omission (failing to do something required, e.g., not reporting a change).
Certain events can reasonably be expected to cause specific results; the nurse should know or reasonably anticipate that injury will probably follow from an act or omission.
The injury resulted directly from the professional’s breach of duty (e.g., proving a specific nurse’s break in aseptic technique caused a healthcare-associated infection).
Physical, financial, or emotional harm that resulted from the breach. A wrong medication that causes no harm does not meet the elements for malpractice.

Compensation awarded to restore the plaintiff’s original position as far as financially possible: medical costs, lost wages, pain and suffering/emotional damages, and punitive damages if conduct was malicious, willful, or wanton.

The level of care a reasonably prudent nurse with similar education and experience would provide in similar circumstances; defined by the NPA and Board rules, job description, agency policies, and national standards (ANA, specialty organizations).

“Let the master answer”: an employer can be held liable for the negligent acts of employees within the scope of employment; a suit naming a nurse usually also names the employer. Employers are also liable for failing to provide adequate staff/resources, education on new equipment, or orientation.
“The thing speaks for itself”: the harm cannot be traced to a specific provider or standard but would not normally occur without negligence (e.g., a surgical instrument left inside a client).
The legal time limit between when the plaintiff knew or should have known of an injury and when a lawsuit must be filed; varies by state and injury type, often extended for minors.
Liability insurance that covers incidents that occurred while the policy was active, regardless of when the claim is filed (even after the policy ends).
Liability insurance that covers an incident only if both the incident occurred and the claim was reported while the policy was active (unless extended “tail” coverage is purchased).
Timely, factual, complete charting according to policy that shows the timeline of care: assessments, interventions, client response, and provider notification of abnormal findings.

sections.heading: Negligence vs. malpractice: whose standard?
sections.body:
Negligence is the general idea: falling below what a reasonable person would do and causing unintended harm — like running a stop sign while distracted. Malpractice is negligence by a professional while performing professional duties. The yardstick changes from “an ordinary reasonable person” to “a reasonably prudent nurse with similar education and experience in similar circumstances.” A critical care nurse is measured against reasonably skilled critical care nurses; an RN is measured against RNs.

Any negligent act or omission by a nurse, however unintentional, can rise to malpractice and jeopardize the license. Nursing students are held to the same standard as an experienced, licensed RN for the care they provide, because the public relies on that expertise. “I’m just a student” is never a defense. The practical lesson: a student (or new nurse) who is unsure how to do something must stop and get help from the instructor or preceptor before acting — doing it anyway and getting it wrong is a breach; asking first is safe practice.

Malpractice can be by commission (doing something wrong: wrong site, wrong dose, wrong client) or omission (failing to do something: not assessing, not reporting, not raising rails, not questioning an unsafe order).

rows: Who
Anyone
A professional acting in a professional role
Standard
Reasonable person
Reasonably prudent professional with similar training
Example
Leaving a wet floor at home that trips a guest
Leaving a high-fall-risk client’s bed raised with no alarm, followed by a fall and hip fracture
Proof
Duty, breach, causation, harm
All malpractice elements, usually with expert testimony about the standard

check.q: A student nurse is told to hang an IV antibiotic she has never prepared. Her instructor is with another client. What should she do?
check.a: Wait and ask the instructor (or the assigned RN) before proceeding. Students are held to the RN standard; proceeding without competence would be a breach.

sections.heading: Box 49.1: the four categories of negligence that become malpractice
sections.body:
Almost every malpractice scenario fits one of four buckets. Learning them helps you spot the omission hidden in a long question stem.

Failure to follow standards of care includes skipping a complete admission assessment or plan of care, not following protocols or policies (such as using an improper injection site), not following verbal or written orders, not providing a safe environment, not monitoring the client’s condition and taking protective action, and not notifying the provider of changes. Failure to communicate and document accurately includes misusing the EHR so the client’s condition is not communicated, and not documenting or reporting assessment findings, lab values, or status changes to the provider and team. Failure to act as a client advocate includes not questioning orders when the client’s condition warrants, not questioning incomplete or illegible orders, and not reporting unsafe practice to the proper people. Failure to supervise adequately includes not knowing the skill level of the people you supervise and not monitoring them.

table.caption: Box 49.1 applied
rows: Failure to follow standards of care
Gives metoprolol without checking an apical pulse of 46
Assesses before giving, holds per parameters, notifies provider
Failure to communicate/document
Charts a potassium of 6.2 but never calls the provider
Reports critical values immediately using SBAR; documents the call and response
Failure to act as advocate
Gives a dose that is 10 times the usual range because “that’s what was ordered”
Holds the dose, clarifies with the prescriber, uses the chain of command if unresolved
Failure to supervise
Delegates vital signs to a new aide and never checks the results on a postoperative client
Knows the aide’s competency, gives clear expectations, follows up on results

bullets: Medication safety alert: before giving any drug, know why the client is receiving it, the acceptable dosage range, possible adverse effects, toxicity levels, and contraindications.

When the provider cannot be reached for a critical finding (e.g., potassium 6.4 mEq/L with peaked T waves after two unanswered pages), documenting and waiting is a failure to act. Keep monitoring the client and escalate through the chain of command — charge nurse, nursing supervisor, then the medical director or rapid response team per policy — documenting each attempt, time, and response.

Advocacy is not optional: “The provider ordered it” is never a defense for giving a dose that is clearly unsafe for this client. Hold, clarify with the prescriber, and escalate if the concern is not resolved; never change the dose yourself.

sections.heading: The six elements of malpractice: all must be proven
sections.body: To establish liability for malpractice, the plaintiff must prove each element. If any one is missing, the claim fails. That is why exam traps love the scenario where a nurse gives the wrong drug but the client is unharmed: there is a breach, but no injury — so no malpractice (even though it is still an error that must be reported and may matter to the Board).

table.caption: Six elements (p. 2828)
rows: 1. Duty
Did the nurse owe care to this client?
The nurse accepted the assignment and received report
2. Breach of duty
Did the nurse deviate from the standard (commission or omission)?
Gave 10 mg instead of 1 mg; did not reassess after a fall
3. Foreseeability
Should a prudent nurse have anticipated harm?
Leaving a sedated client with rails down and no call light in reach
4. Causation
Did the breach directly cause the injury?
The overdose caused respiratory depression requiring intubation
5. Injury or harm
Was there physical, financial, or emotional harm?
Hip fracture, anoxic injury, extended stay
6. Damages
What compensation restores the client?
Medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering; punitive damages if malicious or wanton

sections.analogy: Picture a chain of six links hanging from a hook. The plaintiff must lift the whole chain. Break any single link — no duty (the nurse was not assigned), no causation (the harm came from the disease), or no injury (the error caused no effect) — and the chain falls. When you analyze a question, look for the missing link.

check.q: A nurse gives a client a double dose of acetaminophen. The client has no adverse effects. A family member threatens to sue for malpractice. Which element is missing?
check.a: Injury or harm (and therefore damages). There was a duty and a breach, but without harm, malpractice cannot be established. The nurse must still assess the client, notify the provider, and report the error per policy.

sections.heading: Respondeat superior, res ipsa loquitur, and the statute of limitations
sections.body:
Respondeat superior means the employer answers for the employee’s acts within the scope of employment. A lawsuit naming a nurse generally also names the hospital. Employers are also directly liable when they fail to provide adequate staff or supplies, fail to educate nurses on new equipment or procedures, or fail to orient nurses. This does not make the nurse immune — the nurse remains personally accountable and can be named individually and disciplined by the Board.

Res ipsa loquitur — “the thing speaks for itself” — applies when harm would not normally happen without negligence and the client could not have caused it, but the specific person or standard cannot be identified. The classic example is a surgical sponge or instrument left inside a client; a burn on an anesthetized client’s skin from a positioning device is another. The doctrine helps the plaintiff by shifting the burden to the defendants to explain.

The statute of limitations limits the time between when a client knew (or should have known) of an injury and when a suit must be filed. The course gives typical limits of 1 to 2 years, which vary by state and type of injury, with extended limits for minors. Because suits can be filed years after care, nurses must document as though the chart will be read by a stranger long after they have forgotten the client.

rows: Respondeat superior
The employer is responsible for employees’ acts on the job
Nurse employed by the hospital is sued; the hospital is named too
Res ipsa loquitur
The harm itself proves someone was negligent
Retained instrument; injury under anesthesia with no clear cause
Statute of limitations
There is a deadline to sue
Client discovers an injury and must file within the state’s time limit

check.q: A travel nurse says, “Since the hospital has respondeat superior liability, I don’t need my own malpractice insurance.” Is that correct?
check.a: No. The nurse can still be named individually, the employer may seek reimbursement, employer policies cover only on-the-job acts, and the Board can still discipline. Individual coverage provides broader protection.

sections.heading: Where the standard of care comes from
sections.body:
The standard of care is what a reasonably prudent nurse with similar education and experience would do in similar circumstances. Its primary legal basis is the state Nurse Practice Act and the Board’s administrative rules, which define professional conduct, scope, and the activities allowed for each level of nursing personnel. These laws change, so nurses must stay current.

Additional sources define the standard more specifically: (1) the job description, which defines scope within that employment — employers can limit but cannot expand scope beyond the NPA; (2) agency policies and procedures — and if current evidence-based practice conflicts with policy, the nurse should resolve it proactively through quality-improvement processes rather than ignoring the policy; and (3) prevailing national standards, such as the ANA Standards of Practice and specialty standards (e.g., critical care). In court, expert witnesses testify about what the standard required.

Legal issues also connect to other nursing concepts. Safety: as many as 1 in 10 hospitalized clients experience an adverse event, many involving medications; reporting errors minimizes harm and reveals root causes, while covering errors up carries serious professional and legal consequences. Management and delegation: managers must follow legal requirements, ensure compliance, correct noncompliance, and make sure tasks are delegated appropriately under the NPA and facility policy.

table.caption: Legal issues and related concepts
rows: Cognition
Clients must have capacity to understand benefits, risks, and alternatives; if capacity exists, consent must be voluntary
Give information at the client’s level; work with the team to assess capacity; help with forms and questions; work with a surrogate if capacity is lacking
Comfort
Clients have a legal right to appropriate end-of-life care; hospitals receiving Medicare/Medicaid must provide advance directive information and support
Examine your own biases about EOL care; know EOL options; seek support to advocate; anticipate information families need; recognize advance directives ease family conflict
Communication
Nurses must protect the privacy of all client information in all settings and follow HIPAA
Limit EHR access to appropriate staff; explain privacy protections to clients; discuss care only with appropriate people and not outside the unit

sections.example: A unit policy still calls for routine saline flushes before suctioning, which current evidence no longer supports. The prudent nurse does not simply ignore the policy on her own; she raises the evidence with the unit practice council or manager so the policy is reviewed and updated through quality improvement.

sections.heading: Preventing negligence: medication safety, falls, and error reporting
sections.body:
Medication errors are a leading cause of negligence and malpractice claims. Prevention requires a systems approach involving the whole interprofessional team: clear orders, barcode scanning, independent double checks for high-alert drugs, reconciliation, and a culture where errors and near misses are reported. Errors must be clearly documented in the factual record and disclosed and discussed with the client according to policy. Other risk areas include communicating care concerns, making sure orders are clear, understanding how equipment works, and mentoring and care planning.

Maximizing client safety: older and hospitalized clients can become confused by procedures, medications, and a new environment. Implement safety measures at admission per protocol, teach clients and caregivers the measures and why they matter, attend to every client complaint (never dismiss a sudden severe headache that could signal a brain bleed), and verify client identity with two identifiers at every encounter. Falls are a common cause of injury and of suits against nurses and facilities: assess fall risk and document every measure taken in response to that assessment.

Just Culture: how organizations respond to errors. Most hospitals and many Boards of Nursing judge the behavior behind an event, not just the outcome. Three categories form a continuum: (1) Human error — an inadvertent slip or lapse (picking up the wrong vial that looks like the right one); the response is to console the nurse and fix the system that made the slip easy. (2) At-risk behavior — a choice to take a shortcut whose risk the nurse does not recognize or believes is justified (skipping barcode scanning “because the scanner is slow and nothing bad has happened”); the response is coaching, removing the incentive for the shortcut, and fixing the system problem. (3) Reckless behavior — conscious disregard of a substantial, unjustifiable risk (giving medications while impaired, knowingly falsifying a record); the response is discipline, and reporting to the Board when required. Notice that the outcome does not decide the category: an at-risk shortcut is still at-risk even if no client has been harmed yet. Just Culture is also why honest reporting is protected and covering up an error is treated so seriously.

When an error happens, the safe sequence is consistent.
steps: Assess the client first — vital signs, effects of the error, and immediate safety.
Intervene to minimize harm and notify the provider promptly with the facts.

Document objective facts in the medical record (what was given, assessment findings, provider notification, interventions, client response) — without blame, opinion, or any reference to the incident report.
Complete an incident (occurrence/safety event) report per policy; it is a quality-improvement tool, not part of the chart, and it is not referenced in the chart.
Disclose to the client according to policy, and participate honestly in root-cause review.

check.q: A nurse realizes she gave a client’s 0900 insulin to the wrong client. What is the first action?
check.a: Assess the client who received the insulin (blood glucose, level of consciousness) and treat or prevent hypoglycemia, then notify the provider, document facts, and complete an incident report.

sections.heading: Communication, defensive documentation, and liability insurance
sections.body:
Poor communication combined with a bad outcome raises the risk of a claim. Clients who feel heard and informed sue less often. Clear explanations, attentive listening, and teaching show caring and build trust.

Documentation is the legal record of what happened. If it was not documented, a jury may assume it was not done. Document defensively: timely, objective, complete, according to policy, and showing the timeline of care — assessments, interventions, client response, and provider notification of abnormal labs or status changes, including the provider’s response. Never rely on memory, never chart ahead, never alter or delete an entry (follow the EHR correction process), and chart only your own care. Quote the client when useful. If you notified the provider, record who, when, what was reported, and what was ordered.

Professional liability insurance manages financial risk. Nursing students usually must carry it for their program. Know the two policy types and the two sponsor types.

table.caption: Liability insurance comparisons
rows: Occurrence-based
Any incident that occurred while the policy was active, no matter when the claim is filed
Sued years later after the policy ended? Still covered
Claims-made
Only if the incident occurred AND the claim was reported while the policy was active
Needs “tail” (extended reporting) coverage when the policy ends
Individual
Broadest: 24-hour basis, any setting within scope of practice
Covers volunteer work, off-duty help, and suits where employer interests differ
Employer-sponsored
Narrowest: only actions performed as an employee during work
Does not cover care outside the job

sections.example: Poor entry: “Client doing fine. Doctor aware.” Defensive entry: “1420 BP 84/50, HR 118, client reports dizziness, skin cool and pale. HOB lowered, IV NS infusing at 125 mL/hr. 1425 Dr. Kim notified of findings via phone; order received for 500 mL NS bolus. 1445 bolus started. 1515 BP 104/66, HR 96, client denies dizziness.”

sections.heading: Common traps & look-alikes
sections.body: Each pair below is a classic distractor set.

rows: Breach vs. malpractice
A breach alone is not malpractice; harm caused by the breach is required
“No adverse effects” → no malpractice (still an error to report)
Negligence vs. malpractice
Malpractice is negligence by a professional measured by the professional standard
Nurse acting in a nursing role → malpractice
Foreseeability vs. causation
Foreseeability: harm was predictable; causation: the breach actually produced the harm
“Should have anticipated” vs. “directly resulted from”
Respondeat superior vs. res ipsa loquitur
Employer liability for employees vs. the harm itself implies negligence
“Hospital also named” vs. “retained sponge, unknown who”
Occurrence vs. claims-made
Occurrence covers any incident during the policy period; claims-made needs incident and claim during the policy
“Policy expired before the suit was filed”
Incident report vs. chart entry
Report = QI tool, not mentioned in the chart; chart = objective facts of care
Option says “document that an incident report was filed” → wrong
Employer policy vs. NPA
Policy can limit, never expand, scope
“The unit allows LPNs/aides to…” something outside scope

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: negligence and prevention
sections.body:
Common patterns: (1) Which element is missing (usually harm or causation); (2) which action prevents liability (assessing, reporting, clarifying orders, documenting objectively); (3) after an error, what first (assess the client); (4) best documentation entry (objective, timed, includes provider notification); (5) insurance type comparisons; and (6) advocacy — questioning an order that does not fit the client’s condition.

Sample item (original): The nurse receives an order for digoxin 0.25 mg PO now. The client’s apical pulse is 52, and this morning’s potassium was 3.1 mEq/L. Which action best protects the client and the nurse? A. Give the digoxin and document the pulse. B. Hold the digoxin and notify the provider of the pulse and potassium. C. Give half the dose and recheck the pulse in one hour. D. Hold the digoxin and document the reason in the medication record only.
steps: Read the stem: an order exists, but the client’s data (bradycardia, hypokalemia that increases digoxin toxicity risk) make the order unsafe now.
Identify what is asked: the action that meets the standard of care and fulfills the advocate role.
Spot cues: pulse under 60 and low potassium; foreseeable harm is toxicity and dysrhythmia.
Eliminate A: following an order that is unsafe for the client’s condition is a failure to advocate; documenting does not fix the breach.
Eliminate C: the nurse cannot change a prescribed dose — that is outside scope.
Eliminate D: holding is correct, but failing to notify the provider is a failure to communicate.
Choose B: hold and notify — it protects the client, communicates the findings, and shows the standard of care. Then document the hold, the notification, and the response.
bullets: Reusable strategy: when an order and the client’s condition conflict, the answer is “hold/clarify and notify,” not “give,” “change it yourself,” or “document only.”

sections.heading: Worked case: the unwitnessed fall at 0300
sections.body: Mr. Thompson, 81, was admitted with pneumonia. His admission fall-risk score is high; he takes a sleeping pill and furosemide. At 0300 the nurse finds him on the floor beside the bed. The bed is in the high position, the bed alarm is off, and the call light is on the bedside table out of reach. He says his right hip hurts. His right leg appears shortened and externally rotated. The night-shift assistant says, “I turned off the alarm because it kept going off.”
steps: Recognize cues: high fall risk, sedative and diuretic (urgency at night), alarm off, bed high, call light out of reach, signs of hip fracture.

Analyze the legal elements: the nurse had a duty; failing to ensure fall precautions is a breach; a fall was foreseeable; the fall likely caused the injury; there is harm. All elements of malpractice may be present.
Take action — client first: do not move him until assessed; check airway, LOC, vital signs, injuries, and neuro status; keep him still, get help, and use safe lifting equipment per policy.
Notify the provider immediately with SBAR: fall, findings, suspected hip fracture; anticipate imaging and pain management. Notify the family per policy.

Document objectively: the time found, position, the client’s words, assessment, the environment as found (bed height, alarm status, call light location), notifications, and interventions — not blame or the words “incident report.”
Complete an incident/safety report so the system issue (alarm fatigue, alarm disabled) can be reviewed.
Supervision follow-up: talk with the assistant about the purpose of the alarm and reporting alarm problems to the nurse — the RN remains accountable for supervising delegated care.

check.q: Which piece of the nurse’s earlier care would most strongly defend the nurse in this case?
check.a: Documentation showing a fall-risk assessment at the start of shift and the specific precautions implemented and checked (bed low, alarm on, call light within reach), plus rounding times. The standard is to assess fall risk and document the measures taken.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Scope and accountability: The NC Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq.) and NCBON rules — 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN) — are the primary basis of the standard of care in NC. The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment; the LPN participates under RN or provider supervision. The RN may delegate tasks, but not the nursing process or nursing judgment. NC has two aide levels: Nurse Aide I (registry kept by NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation) and Nurse Aide II (registry kept by the NCBON; must also be listed on the NA I registry; may perform some advanced tasks such as sterile dressing changes and oxygen therapy per the NCBON NA II task list). A task must be on the aide’s approved list and the RN must decide delegation is appropriate for that specific client. The NCBON “Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP” guides that decision. Failure to supervise is a malpractice category — it applies here.

Just Culture: The NCBON uses a Just Culture–based Complaint Evaluation Tool for practice events, classifying them as human error (console and fix the system), at-risk behavior (coach), or reckless behavior (discipline). Conduct issues — drug diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary or sexual misconduct, confidentiality breaches — are reported to the Board rather than handled only by the employer. The NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.

Lawsuit rules: The NC medical malpractice statute of limitations is generally 3 years, with a 4-year statute of repose (G.S. 1-15(c)) — longer than the 1–2 years cited as typical in the course material. NC is one of the few jurisdictions that keeps pure contributory negligence as a defense, meaning a plaintiff who contributed to their own injury may be barred from recovery. Neither changes the nurse’s duty: practice to the standard and document it.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 49 study guide, pp. 2825–2828 (malpractice statistics, unintentional torts, Box 49.1, six elements, medication safety alert, respondeat superior, res ipsa loquitur, statute of limitations) and pp. 2829–2831 (related concepts table, prevention strategies, falls safety alert, liability insurance, standard of care).

Clarifications: (1) Many legal texts list four elements of negligence (duty, breach, causation, damages); this course lists six by separating foreseeability and injury/harm. Both describe the same idea — learn the six for this course. (2) The course cites 1 to 2 years as a typical statute of limitations; this is state-specific. In North Carolina it is generally 3 years with a 4-year statute of repose. (3) The error-response sequence (assess the client first; incident report is not mentioned in the chart), SBAR, two client identifiers, and “tail” coverage for claims-made policies are standard national practice added to support application. (4) NC delegation and NCBON Just Culture content was added from verified NCBON information. (5) The national Just Culture categories (human error, at-risk behavior, reckless behavior) and chain-of-command escalation when a provider cannot be reached are standard patient-safety practice added to support application; they are not in the course text.

mnemonics.name: “Doctors Bring Four Coffees In Dallas”
mnemonics.text: The six malpractice elements in order: Duty, Breach, Foreseeability, Causation, Injury/harm, Damages. Missing any one breaks the case.

mnemonics.name: Occurrence = “Once covered, always covered”
mnemonics.text: If it happened during the policy, you are covered whenever the claim arrives. Claims-made = both the event and the claim must fall inside the policy window.

pearls: Wrong drug, no harm = breach without malpractice — but still assess, notify, document, and report.
Nursing students are held to the licensed-RN standard: if unsure, stop and ask.
After an error, assess the client first; paperwork comes after safety.
Never write “incident report completed” in the chart; document objective facts of care.
Hold and clarify an order that conflicts with the client’s condition; notify the provider — do not change the dose yourself.
Respondeat superior adds the employer to the suit; it does not remove the nurse’s personal accountability.
Document fall-risk assessment and every precaution taken — that record is the defense.
Individual liability coverage is broadest; employer coverage protects only on-the-job acts.
redFlags: A critical lab value or change in condition that is charted but not communicated to the provider.
An order that is illegible, incomplete, or outside the usual dose range for the client.
A delegated task whose results the RN never reviews, especially for an unstable client.
Alarms turned off, bed high, or call light out of reach for a high-fall-risk client.
Pressure from anyone to alter, delay, or omit documentation of an error.
recap: Negligence = falling below the reasonable-person standard; malpractice = professional negligence measured by the reasonably prudent nurse.
All six elements — duty, breach, foreseeability, causation, injury/harm, damages — must be proven for liability.
Box 49.1 categories: failure to follow standards, to communicate/document, to advocate, and to supervise.
Respondeat superior makes employers liable too; res ipsa loquitur lets the harm itself suggest negligence; statutes of limitations set filing deadlines.
The NPA and Board rules are the primary legal basis of the standard of care, refined by job description, policy, and national standards.
Prevent claims with medication safety, fall prevention, honest error reporting, clear communication, and defensive documentation.
Occurrence policies cover incidents during the policy period no matter when the claim is filed; claims-made requires both within the policy period.

checks.q: A nurse delegates ambulation of a client 2 hours after hip surgery to an aide without checking the client’s orthostatic vital signs. The client faints and fractures a wrist. Which Box 49.1 category applies and which elements are present?
checks.a: Failure to supervise (and to follow standards). Duty, breach, foreseeability (postoperative orthostatic risk), causation, injury, and damages are all plausibly present.

checks.q: A client discovers 3 years after surgery that a sponge was left in her abdomen. Which doctrines might apply?
checks.a: Res ipsa loquitur (harm implies negligence without identifying who), respondeat superior (the hospital is liable for employees), and the statute of limitations (starting when she knew or should have known of the injury).

checks.q: A nurse switches jobs and drops a claims-made policy. Two years later she is sued for care given under that policy. Is she covered?
checks.a: No, unless she bought tail coverage — a claims-made policy requires the claim to be made while the policy is active. An occurrence policy would have covered it.

checks.q: A client’s glucose is 42 mg/dL. The nurse treats it and rechecks, but never charts the event. Why is this a legal problem even though care was correct?
checks.a: Documentation is the legal record; without it, there is no evidence the assessment, treatment, and follow-up were done — failure to document is itself a Box 49.1 category.

checks.q: A unit policy conflicts with a newer national guideline. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Follow the policy while raising the evidence through the proper quality-improvement process (manager, practice council) so the policy can be updated; do not change practice unilaterally.

checks.q: Which is the better entry: “Client upset and uncooperative” or “Client stated, ‘I’m not taking that pill,’ and turned away; purpose of medication explained; provider notified at 1015”? Why?
checks.a: The second — it is objective, quotes the client, and shows teaching and provider notification with a time.

checks.q: A nurse grabs a look-alike vial of heparin instead of saline from a cluttered drawer; a second nurse routinely skips the barcode scan because “it slows me down”; a third nurse comes to work impaired. Using Just Culture, classify each and name the expected response.
checks.a: First nurse: human error (an inadvertent slip) — console and fix the system (separate look-alike vials). Second nurse: at-risk behavior (a shortcut whose risk is underestimated) — coach and remove the incentive/fix the slow scanner. Third nurse: reckless behavior (conscious disregard of substantial risk) — discipline and report to the Board as required.

topics.title: Consent, Competency & Laws Across the Lifespan
topics.summary: Informed consent is the client’s right to understand and accept or refuse care; the provider performing the procedure obtains it, and the nurse assesses understanding, arranges interpretation, and witnesses. Other key laws — competency and surrogates, minor consent, the Controlled Substances Act, Good Samaritan and whistleblower protections, and mandatory abuse reporting — guide nursing actions from childhood through older adulthood.
objectives: Identify the five required elements of informed consent and the separate roles of the provider and the nurse.
Differentiate expressed, implied, and informed consent and apply the emergency doctrine and its exception.
Distinguish legal competency from decision-specific capacity and identify the correct decision maker (client, guardian, surrogate, parent).
Determine when a minor may consent independently and respond to conflicts between adolescents and parents.
Apply the Controlled Substances Act schedules to safe handling, counting, wasting, and diversion reporting.
Explain the conditions for Good Samaritan and whistleblower protection.
Carry out mandated reporting of suspected child abuse and protect adolescent confidentiality appropriately.
topics.bigPicture:
Consent is the legal line between care and battery. Every day the nurse checks that a consent form is signed — but the real job is bigger: making sure the client can see, hear, read, and understand; that an official interpreter is used; that nobody is pressured; and that a client who has questions about the procedure gets them answered by the person doing it. When the client cannot decide, the nurse must know who can — a court-appointed guardian, a health care agent, a surrogate, or a parent — and when the law lets a minor decide alone.

This topic also covers laws that protect people who cannot protect themselves (mandatory child-abuse reporting), that control dangerous drugs (the Controlled Substances Act), and that protect nurses who do the right thing (Good Samaritan and whistleblower laws). Each comes with a condition the NCLEX loves to test: emergency consent does not override a prior refusal; Good Samaritan protection does not apply on the job or if you abandon the victim; whistleblowers must use internal channels first; and abuse reports require suspicion, not proof.

Across the lifespan, the same principle applies: respect the autonomy of anyone who has capacity, protect those who lack it, and follow the law that defines who decides. The questions will give you a client, an age, a situation, and a decision — your job is to pick the person and the process the law recognizes.

keyTerms.def: The client’s legal and ethical right to be informed of, and to give or refuse permission for, any healthcare procedure or treatment; must be given voluntarily without pressure, fear, or undue influence.
An oral or written agreement to a procedure or treatment.

Consent shown by the client’s actions — verbally indicating participation or nonverbally acting consistently with care (e.g., rolling up a sleeve or positioning for an injection, cooperating with vital signs). Also assumed in true emergencies under the emergency doctrine.

Most states presume consent when a person is in imminent danger of loss of life or limb and cannot give informed consent; it does NOT allow a treatment the person previously refused (e.g., blood refused on religious grounds).
A legal presumption that adults (typically age 18) have the right to negotiate contracts and make healthcare decisions unless a court finds otherwise.
A clinical, decision-specific judgment that a person can understand information, appreciate consequences, reason, and communicate a choice; can fluctuate over time.

A court order declaring an adult incompetent (e.g., debilitating brain injury, profound intellectual disability) and appointing a guardian, who must give providers a copy of the order validating decision authority.
Loss of decision-making ability caused temporarily by narcotics or serious illness, or gradually by dementia; the nurse alerts the provider when competency is questionable.

A person authorized by law, advance directive, or agency policy to make decisions when the client lacks capacity (e.g., health care agent under a power of attorney, guardian, next of kin per state hierarchy).
A minor no longer under parental control who manages their own financial affairs (or is otherwise emancipated under state law) and may consent to their own care.
A minor whom state law allows to give valid consent because they can understand the risks and benefits of a treatment; recognition varies by state.

Federal law enforced by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) that classifies drugs into Schedules I–V by medical use, abuse potential, and safety; requires DEA registration and strict recordkeeping from manufacture to dispensing.

State laws that encourage healthcare professionals to help in emergencies by protecting them from liability when they volunteer outside an employment contract, provided they act within the standard of their training and do not abandon the victim.
An employee’s disclosure of an employer’s unsafe or illegal practices or policies.
The employee who reports the employer’s unsafe or illegal practices; protected from retaliation when legal conditions are met.
A person legally required to report suspected abuse or neglect; nurses must report reasonable suspicion of child maltreatment in good faith without needing proof.

sections.heading: Informed consent: five elements and who does what
sections.body:
Informed consent protects the client’s right to decide. It is valid only when the client has capacity, receives adequate information, and agrees voluntarily — without pressure, fear, or undue influence. Consent is required for elective and therapeutic surgery, diagnostic procedures, and procedures involving sedation or anesthesia; it is not required for time-sensitive, lifesaving emergency procedures.

The provider performing the procedure (usually the physician, surgeon, or advanced practice provider) is responsible for explaining the procedure and obtaining informed consent. The nurse does not explain the risks of surgery to make consent valid. The nurse’s role is to assess the client’s ability to see, hear, and read; arrange an official medical interpreter when needed (never a family member, who may filter information and compromises privacy); consider cultural and spiritual preferences; and witness the signature. Witnessing means confirming the person signing is the client (or legal decision maker), that the signature is voluntary, and that the client appears to understand. If the client says, “I’m not really sure what they’re doing,” or seems pressured, the nurse does not proceed with witnessing — the nurse notifies the provider, who must return to explain.

A client may withdraw consent at any time, even after signing. If a client withdraws consent, the nurse stops, notifies the provider, and documents. Premedication with opioids or sedatives before consent is signed can invalidate it — consent is obtained before sedating drugs.

table.caption: Five mandatory elements of informed consent
rows: 1. Reason
Why treatment is needed — the presenting problem or diagnosis
2. Procedure
The specific procedure or treatment proposed
3. Benefits and experience
How it will help and what the client can expect during and after
4. Risks
Possible negative side effects or outcomes
5. Alternatives
Other options, including declining treatment, with advantages and disadvantages of each

check.q: Just before signing a surgical consent, a client asks the nurse, “Will this surgery leave a big scar? What are the chances it won’t work?” What should the nurse do?
check.a: Hold off on witnessing and notify the surgeon that the client has unanswered questions about the procedure; the provider must explain risks and outcomes before consent is valid.

sections.heading: Expressed, implied, and emergency consent
sections.body:
Expressed consent is stated out loud or in writing. Implied consent is shown by behavior: a client who holds out an arm when the nurse says, “I’m going to check your blood pressure,” or who rolls onto the side for an injection. Implied consent covers routine, low-risk care; it does not replace informed consent for procedures.

In an emergency, the law presumes consent when a person faces imminent danger to life or limb and cannot consent (e.g., unconscious after trauma). The critical exception: the emergency doctrine does not permit a treatment the client previously refused. If a conscious, competent adult who is a Jehovah’s Witness refused blood products — and especially if that refusal is documented in an advance directive or a wallet card — giving blood after the client becomes unconscious is battery, even in a life-threatening hemorrhage. The team instead uses alternatives the client accepts (volume expanders, cell-saver if acceptable, medications to reduce bleeding) and involves ethics and legal resources as needed.

Remember that capacity can be decision-specific: a client with mild cognitive impairment might be able to consent to a flu shot but not to complex surgery. Cognitive impairment does not automatically mean a client cannot consent unless a court has declared the person legally incompetent.

check.q: An unconscious client arrives after a crash with massive bleeding. The ED nurse finds a signed card in the wallet refusing all blood transfusions. What applies?
check.a: The emergency doctrine does not override a known prior refusal. Report the card to the provider immediately; blood should not be given; use acceptable alternatives and follow policy.

sections.heading: Competency, capacity, guardians, and surrogates
sections.body:
Competency is a legal status: every adult (typically 18 and older) is presumed competent unless a court rules otherwise. When a court declares an adult legally incompetent (e.g., debilitating brain injury, profound intellectual disability), it appoints a guardian, who must give the healthcare team a copy of the court order. The nurse verifies that order is in the record before accepting the guardian’s decisions.

Capacity is a clinical judgment, made by the provider and team, about whether a person can understand, appreciate, reason, and communicate a choice for a specific decision at a specific time. Temporary incompetency can come from opioids, sedation, serious illness, hypoglycemia, or delirium; it can come gradually from dementia. If capacity is questionable, the nurse alerts the provider and does not let an unclear client sign. If the client lacks capacity, decisions go to a surrogate per law and agency policy — often the agent named in a health care power of attorney, then a guardian or family per state hierarchy.

Advance directives speak for clients who lose capacity. Under the federal Patient Self-Determination Act, hospitals that receive Medicare/Medicaid funds must ask clients about advance directives and provide information; nurses support those wishes and recognize that directives give peace of mind and reduce family conflict. A living will describes the treatments the person wants or refuses; a health care power of attorney names an agent to decide.
steps: Presume the adult client is competent and has the right to decide.
Watch for cues of reduced capacity: new confusion, sedation, inability to repeat back information, fluctuating attention.
Report concerns to the provider before consent is signed; do not have a client sign while sedated or confused.
If a guardian is involved, confirm a copy of the court order is on the chart.
If the client lacks capacity and has no guardian, identify the surrogate per advance directive, state law, and policy.
Give information at the client’s cognitive level and include the client in the discussion as much as possible.
sections.example: A client with early Alzheimer disease is scheduled for cataract surgery. She can explain why the surgery is needed, what will happen, and that she could keep wearing thick glasses instead. Even with a dementia diagnosis, she demonstrates capacity for this decision and may sign her own consent. Her daughter’s preference does not override her choice.

sections.heading: Minors and consent: the rule and the exceptions
sections.body:
For a minor (under 18), a parent or legal guardian generally gives informed consent. A minor may consent independently when: the emergency doctrine applies; the minor is emancipated (no longer under parental control and managing own finances, or otherwise emancipated under state law); state law recognizes a mature minor able to understand the risks (some states, for some 14- and 15-year-olds); a court order authorizes treatment; or the law lets a minor consent to a specific service — for example, a minor parent consenting for their own child, or state allowances for contraception, prenatal care, mental health care, STI care, or substance use treatment.

Box 49.2 shows how much states vary: contraception (27 states + DC allow all minors, from age 12 or 14); STIs (45 states + DC allow all minors age 12+, a few from 14, SC from 16); prenatal care (33 states + DC; 14 of these let providers inform parents in the minor’s best interest); adoption placement (28 states + DC allow minor parents); medical care for the minor’s own child (30 states + DC); and abortion (2 states + DC allow all minors; 21 require at least one parent’s consent; 10 require parental notification). The exam lesson: know your state, and when a law lets the minor consent, the nurse treats the minor as the decision maker for that service.

Clinical Example A — Marvin, 15, with acute myelocytic leukemia, is out of his second remission. He agrees to a bone marrow transplant if a donor is found, but refuses resuscitation and life support, supported by the chaplain and social worker. His parents want every effort. The nurse should know the state’s mature-minor law and agency policy, facilitate open communication among Marvin, his parents, the provider, social worker, chaplain, and ethics committee, and advocate for Marvin’s voice while respecting legal limits. The nurse does not decide the conflict alone, and does not dismiss Marvin because he is a minor.

check.q: A 16-year-old who is the mother of a 6-month-old brings the infant for immunizations. Who consents for the infant?
check.a: In states that allow minor parents to consent for their child, the 16-year-old parent consents. The infant’s grandparent does not consent unless they are the legal guardian.

sections.heading: The Controlled Substances Act: schedules and nursing responsibility
sections.body:
The CSA is federal law enforced by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). It classifies drugs into Schedules I–V based on accepted medical use, abuse potential, and dependence risk; requires DEA registration for prescribers and dispensers; and requires tight recordkeeping that tracks drugs from manufacture to the client. For nurses, the CSA becomes daily practice: controlled drugs are stored securely (automated dispensing cabinet or double-locked), counted per policy, signed out to a specific client, and wasted with a licensed witness who actually observes the waste. Discrepancies are reported immediately, not “fixed” later.

Diversion red flags in a coworker include frequent waste without witnesses, high doses pulled for clients whose pain seems uncontrolled, volunteering to give others’ opioids, frequent bathroom breaks, and changes in behavior. Diversion is a crime, endangers clients, and must be reported through the chain of command and to the Board as required. Possession of a controlled drug without a valid prescription is a criminal act.

check.q: The nurse gives 2 mg of a 4-mg morphine syringe. A coworker offers to cosign the waste later because she is busy. What should the nurse do?
check.a: Not accept a cosign without observation. The witness must observe the waste; wait for or find another licensed witness and follow policy.

sections.heading: Good Samaritan laws and whistleblowing
sections.body:
Good Samaritan laws encourage healthcare professionals to help in emergencies by protecting them from liability when they volunteer their skills outside an employment contract. To stay protected, the nurse must (1) give care consistent with their training and licensure — not perform procedures beyond their scope (e.g., a nurse should not attempt a field tracheostomy), and (2) once care has begun, follow through: stay until the victim is placed in the care of someone able to provide appropriate care, such as EMS. Leaving the victim after starting care is abandonment. Protection generally does not apply to care given as part of paid employment, to care for which the nurse is compensated, or to gross negligence or willful misconduct.

Whistleblowing is an employee’s disclosure of unsafe or illegal employer practices; the employee is the whistleblower. The course cites the Whistleblower Protection Act of 1989 and OSHA. Strictly, the 1989 Act protects federal employees; most hospital nurses are protected instead by OSHA-administered whistleblower provisions and by state laws, whose details and filing deadlines vary. The practical sequence below is the same either way. To qualify for protection, the course teaches that the employee must (1) first make every effort to resolve the problem through the employer’s internal reporting procedures — unless already threatened or retaliated against; (2) report a violation of a specific law or rule (not a simple error), with the employer aware and given written notice and reasonable time to correct it (or the employee reports, or threatens to report, to the appropriate agency); and (3) know that retaliation — firing, demotion, discipline, intimidation — is prohibited. To prevail in a retaliation claim, the employee should report the retaliation to OSHA before resigning, and within the filing deadline.

steps: Document the unsafe practice factually (dates, times, what happened, the rule involved).
Report through the chain of command and internal reporting system (charge nurse, manager, compliance/risk).
Give written notice and allow reasonable time for correction.
If not corrected, or if retaliation occurs, report to the appropriate state or federal agency.
If retaliation occurs, file with OSHA promptly and before resigning.

check.q: A nurse on vacation stops at a crash, starts CPR, then leaves when a bystander says “I know CPR too” before EMS arrives. Is the nurse protected?
check.a: Possibly not — leaving before care is transferred to someone qualified to provide appropriate care can be abandonment. The nurse should stay until EMS takes over.

sections.heading: Across the lifespan: child abuse reporting and adolescent confidentiality
sections.body:
Nurses are mandated reporters of suspected child abuse — physical, emotional, and sexual maltreatment (and neglect). The nurse reports according to organizational policy and personally reports to the proper authority, and documents all pertinent information in the medical record. Reporting suspected abuse is an exception to confidentiality. The nurse does not need proof — the burden of proof belongs to investigators. The nurse reports the facts and circumstances that led to the suspicion, in good faith and without malicious intent; the reporter’s identity is generally not disclosed to the suspected abuser. Failure to report can bring civil (and in many states, criminal) consequences.

Clinical signs: in infants, any bruising suggests physical abuse (non-mobile infants rarely bruise), and vomiting, irritability, and lethargy may indicate head injury. In older children, look for unexplained injuries, injuries that do not match the explanation or developmental stage, and untreated medical problems. Sexual abuse often leaves no abnormal physical findings, though cultures may reveal an STI; the history from an abusive caregiver may be vague or misleading. Interview and document in the child’s own words, ensure safety, and avoid leading questions.

Older and vulnerable adults are protected by the same reporting logic. Signs of neglect or abuse include untreated pressure injuries, poor hygiene, soiled bedding, dehydration or weight loss, an empty refrigerator, missed medications, unexplained bruises or fractures, fearfulness around a caregiver, and sudden financial changes. When the nurse has reasonable cause to believe a disabled or vulnerable adult needs protection, the nurse reports to adult protective services per agency policy and state law — again without investigating, demanding proof, or threatening the caregiver — and then addresses the client’s immediate needs, documents objectively, and notifies the provider. Teaching the caregiver a turning schedule may be part of the plan later, but it does not replace the report when the client is already being harmed.

Adolescents seeking care for contraception, sexual health, substance use, or mental health need honest confidentiality. Tell the adolescent that confidentiality will be kept when possible, but not in every circumstance — for example, when there is risk of serious harm to self or others, when abuse must be reported, or when billing and benefits statements sent to a parent’s insurance may reveal the service. Never promise “I won’t tell anyone, no matter what.”
steps: Recognize cues: injury inconsistent with history or development, delayed care, bruising in an infant, changing stories.
Ensure the child’s immediate safety and treat injuries.
Document objective findings and statements in the child’s and caregiver’s own words; use body diagrams per policy.
Report the suspicion per agency policy and directly to the designated child protective agency — do not wait for proof or for a provider’s permission.
Do not confront or accuse the caregiver or conduct your own investigation.
Cooperate with investigators and continue to provide nonjudgmental care.

check.q: A 15-year-old asks the nurse, “If I tell you something, do you promise you won’t tell my mom?” What is the best response?
check.a: Be honest: “Most of what you tell me stays private, but if you or someone else is in danger or being hurt, I have to share it to keep you safe.” Do not promise absolute confidentiality.

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this: consent and protective laws
sections.body:
Expect: (1) nurse’s role in consent — what to do when the client has questions, is sedated, or needs an interpreter; (2) who may consent — a minor, an emancipated minor, a guardian, a surrogate; (3) emergency doctrine exceptions; (4) mandated reporting — the first or best action when abuse is suspected; (5) Good Samaritan conditions; (6) controlled substance handling — waste, count discrepancies, diversion; and (7) needs further teaching about any of these.

Sample item (original): A client who speaks Vietnamese is scheduled for a cardiac catheterization. The client’s adult son, who speaks English and Vietnamese, offers to translate the consent discussion so the procedure can start on time. Which action should the nurse take? A. Allow the son to interpret because he is fluent and trusted by the client. B. Contact a qualified medical interpreter for the provider’s consent discussion. C. Ask the client to nod if they agree, then witness the signature. D. Provide a Vietnamese copy of the form and witness the signature.
steps: Read the stem: language barrier; family offering to interpret; consent for an invasive procedure.
Identify what is asked: the nurse’s role in ensuring valid informed consent.
Spot cues: “son offers to translate” — family interpreters may filter or soften information and compromise privacy.
Eliminate A: fluency does not make a family member an appropriate medical interpreter.
Eliminate C: a nod is not informed consent; the client has not understood the five elements.
Eliminate D: a translated form alone does not replace the provider’s explanation and the client’s chance to ask questions.
Choose B: a qualified medical interpreter ensures accurate, private communication; the provider explains and the nurse then witnesses.
bullets: Reusable strategy: in consent items, ask “Has the client truly understood, from the person doing the procedure, without pressure?” If not, the answer is the action that fixes the gap (interpreter, notify provider, delay sedation).

sections.heading: Worked case: the bruised infant and the busy afternoon
sections.body: A 4-month-old is brought to the pediatric clinic by her mother’s boyfriend for “fussiness and throwing up.” The infant is lethargic and irritable. The nurse notices fingertip-shaped bruises on both upper arms. The boyfriend says the baby “rolled off the couch yesterday.” The infant cannot yet roll over. The provider is running behind and says, “Let’s get her to the ED for a head CT; we’ll sort out the bruises later.” The boyfriend asks the nurse to “keep this between us — her mom will freak out.”
steps: Recognize cues: bruising in a non-mobile infant; vomiting, irritability, lethargy (possible head injury); explanation inconsistent with development.
Prioritize: physiologic safety first — this infant may have intracranial injury. Arrange emergency transport and monitor airway, breathing, and neuro status.

Recognize the legal duty: the nurse is a mandated reporter. The suspicion is reasonable; proof is not needed, and the provider’s plan to “sort it out later” does not remove the nurse’s personal duty to report.
Report per policy and directly to the designated child protective agency (in NC, the county DSS) — promptly, not after investigating.
Do not promise the boyfriend confidentiality and do not confront or accuse him; maintain a calm, nonjudgmental approach.
Document objectively: the bruise pattern, size, location (body diagram), the caregiver’s exact words, the infant’s behavior, vital signs, notifications, and the report made (time, agency, person).
Communicate to the ED via handoff so the receiving team is aware of the safety concern.

check.q: Later, the boyfriend asks who made the report. How should the nurse respond?
check.a: The reporter’s identity is generally confidential. The nurse does not reveal it and can explain that the team’s focus is the baby’s safety and care.

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.body:
Child maltreatment — universal reporting: Under G.S. 7B-301, any person or institution with cause to suspect that a juvenile (under 18) is abused, neglected, or dependent, or has died from maltreatment, must report to the county department of social services (DSS) director. Knowingly failing to report is a crime. Report suspicion; do not investigate or wait for proof. Good-faith reporters are immune. (Note: the general course statement that failure to report “may result in civil charges” is stronger in NC, where it is criminal.)

Disabled or vulnerable adults: Under G.S. 108A-102, any person with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to the county DSS director, orally or in writing; good-faith reporters are immune.

Minor consent: Under G.S. 90-21.5, a minor may give effective consent for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of (1) venereal/sexually transmitted and other reportable diseases, (2) pregnancy — but not sterilization or abortion, (3) abuse of controlled substances or alcohol, and (4) emotional disturbance. Emancipated minors may consent. The age of majority is 18.

Good Samaritan: G.S. 90-21.14 protects a person who gives emergency first aid or treatment without compensation unless the injury results from gross negligence, wanton conduct, or intentional wrongdoing; it does not cover care in the normal course of paid employment.

Advance directives: NC recognizes the Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3) and the Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death (living will, G.S. 90-321). The portable medical order form is the MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment). Conduct issues such as diversion of controlled substances are reported to the NCBON; the Board offers alternative-to-discipline programs for substance use.

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body:
Source: Module 49 study guide, pp. 2831–2832 (informed, expressed, and implied consent; capacity; competency; emergency doctrine), pp. 2832–2833 (minors, Box 49.2, Clinical Example A, Controlled Substances Act and Table 49.2, Good Samaritan and whistleblowing laws), and p. 2834 (infants, children, adolescents; high-yield traps).

Clarifications: (1) The CSA is enforced by the Drug Enforcement Administration (the course says “Agency”). (2) Table 49.2 lists Schedule V as “no Rx required.” In practice, many Schedule V drugs (e.g., pregabalin, lacosamide) require a prescription; only certain low-dose codeine products may be sold without a prescription under pharmacist control where state law allows. Ezogabine, listed as a Schedule V example, was discontinued in the U.S. in 2017, so pregabalin is used as the example here. (3) Schedule I drugs have no currently accepted federal medical use; federal rescheduling of marijuana to Schedule III has been under review since 2024 — check its current status; the NCLEX tests the schedule concepts, not this policy change. (4) The course says failure to report child abuse may result in civil charges; many states, including NC, also make knowing failure to report a crime. (5) The Whistleblower Protection Act of 1989 applies to federal employees; other nurses are protected through OSHA-administered whistleblower provisions and state laws. Protections differ by statute and include filing deadlines; the internal-first sequence taught here is the course standard and matches NCLEX chain-of-command expectations. (6) Vulnerable-adult abuse and neglect reporting to adult protective services was added as standard national practice to complete the lifespan content.
