mnemonics.name: RPBRA — the five consent elements
mnemonics.text: Reason, Procedure, Benefits, Risks, Alternatives (including no treatment). “Real Patients Bravely Review Alternatives.”

mnemonics.name: Good Samaritan = “Free, Fit, Finish”
mnemonics.text: Free (no pay, not on duty), Fit (within your training), Finish (stay until qualified help takes over).

mnemonics.name: Abuse reporting = “Suspect, Secure, Spell it out, Send”
mnemonics.text: Suspect (reasonable suspicion is enough), Secure the child’s safety, Spell it out in objective documentation, Send the report to the designated agency.

pearls: The provider obtains consent; the nurse witnesses and verifies understanding — if questions remain, notify the provider.
Use a qualified medical interpreter, never a family member, for consent.
Get consent before giving sedating or opioid premedication.
Emergency consent never overrides a known prior refusal of that treatment.
A diagnosis of dementia or mental illness does not automatically remove a client’s right to consent; capacity is decision-specific.
Guardians must provide a copy of the court order; confirm it is on the chart.
Report suspected child abuse on suspicion — not proof — and do not confront the caregiver.
Tell adolescents confidentiality is kept when possible but not guaranteed (safety, abuse, insurance statements).
redFlags: A client signing consent after receiving an opioid or sedative, or while confused.
A family member interpreting for the consent discussion.
Bruising on a non-mobile infant or an injury that does not match the history.
A controlled-substance count discrepancy or an unwitnessed waste.
An off-duty nurse leaving an emergency victim before qualified help arrives.
recap: Informed consent needs capacity, the five elements (reason, procedure, benefits, risks, alternatives), and voluntariness.
The provider doing the procedure obtains consent; the nurse assesses ability to understand, arranges an interpreter, and witnesses.
Expressed consent is spoken or written; implied consent is shown by actions or presumed in emergencies — except for a previously refused treatment.
Competency is legal (court-appointed guardian if lost); capacity is a clinical, decision-specific judgment.
Minors need parental consent unless emancipated, mature-minor law applies, a court orders care, it is an emergency, or a law allows the specific service.
The CSA (DEA) assigns Schedules I–V; nurses secure, count, document, waste with a witness, and report discrepancies.
Good Samaritan protection requires volunteer, off-duty care within training and no abandonment; whistleblowers report internally first.
Nurses must report suspected child abuse in good faith without proof; confidentiality does not block the report.

checks.q: A client received hydromorphone 30 minutes ago and is drowsy when the surgeon arrives with the consent form for a nonemergency procedure. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Tell the surgeon the client recently received an opioid and is drowsy; consent should be delayed until the client has capacity, because consent signed while sedated may not be valid.

checks.q: A 17-year-old who is married and lives independently needs an appendectomy. Who signs the consent?
checks.a: The client, as an emancipated minor (marriage and independent living are typical emancipation criteria).

checks.q: A client with schizophrenia who is not under guardianship refuses a flu vaccine and explains why clearly. Can the nurse give it on the psychiatrist’s order?
checks.a: No. Mental illness does not by itself remove the right to refuse; he demonstrates capacity for this decision. Giving it would be battery. Document and notify the provider.

checks.q: An off-duty nurse at a restaurant helps a choking man and is later sued. What determines protection?
checks.a: Whether the care was voluntary and uncompensated, within her training, free of gross negligence or willful misconduct, and continued until qualified help arrived.

checks.q: A nurse notices a colleague often signs out oxycodone for clients who later say they didn’t receive pain medication. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Report the concern through the chain of command (manager, pharmacy/risk) promptly and factually; diversion endangers clients and is reported to the Board as required. Do not confront or investigate alone.

checks.q: A 14-year-old requests STI testing and asks that her parents not be told. In most states, how should the nurse respond?
checks.a: Most states allow minors to consent to STI care; provide care confidentially within the law and explain honestly the limits of confidentiality (e.g., insurance statements, safety concerns).

checks.q: During a home visit, the nurse finds an older adult with dementia in soiled bedding with a new pressure injury and no food in the house. The caregiver says, “She refuses help.” What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Report suspected neglect to adult protective services (in NC, the county DSS director) per policy — reasonable cause is enough, proof is not needed. Address the client’s immediate needs, document objective findings and the caregiver’s exact words, and notify the provider. Do not threaten or investigate.
